Because $\angle BOE + \angle COE = \angle BOC$, $$\frac{2}{3}\angle COE + \angle COE = 40^\circ,$$ so $\angle COE = 24^\circ$. (2) When ray $OE$ is below $AB$, $\angle BOE = \frac{2}{3}\angle COE$. Because $\angle COE - \angle BOE = \angle BOC$, $$\angle COE - \frac{2}{3}\angle COE = 40^\circ,$$ so $\angle COE = 120^\circ$. Therefore, $\angle COE$ can be either $24^\circ$ or $120^\circ$.

(1) When ray $OE$ is above $AB$, $\angle BOE = \frac{2}{3}\angle COE$.
Because $\angle BOE + \angle COE = \angle BOC$,
$$\frac{2}{3}\angle COE + \angle COE = 40^\circ,$$
so $\angle COE = 24^\circ$.

(2) When ray $OE$ is below $AB$, $\angle BOE = \frac{2}{3}\angle COE$.
Because $\angle COE - \angle BOE = \angle BOC$,
$$\angle COE - \frac{2}{3}\angle COE = 40^\circ,$$
so $\angle COE = 120^\circ$.

Therefore, $\angle COE$ can be either $24^\circ$ or $120^\circ$.

ready3_open_rewrite.final_cot:
Image description: The figure gives a horizontal segment AB, point O is between A and B, A is on the left and B is on the right; ray OC is drawn from O toward the upper right, and ray OD is drawn from O toward the upper left. OE is not fixedly drawn in the figure; only the basic configuration is given; there is also a similar spare diagram beside it.
Reasoning: It is known that ∠BOC = 40°, and construct OE so that ∠BOE = (2/3)∠COE. Let x = ∠COE. Since the position of OE is not uniquely fixed, cases need to be discussed.
Case 1: OE is inside ∠BOC, that is, above AB and between OB and OC. At this time ∠BOE and ∠COE are adjacent and form ∠BOC, so (2/3)x + x = 40°. Therefore (5/3)x = 40°, x = 24°.
Case 2: OE is below AB, on the other side of OB. At this time the angle from OC to OE contains ∠COB and ∠BOE, so x = 40° + ∠BOE = 40° + (2/3)x. Thus x - (2/3)x = 40°, (1/3)x = 40°, x = 120°.
So ∠COE can be 24° or 120°.
